draft.change: Add a noun article for the gentilic פַּתְרֻסִים. Its geographic base accounts for the ס that the proposed root פתר leaves unexplained. The genealogy supports a people name and gives no basis for the source gloss “labour; service.”
draft.definition: The Pathrusim are the people of Pathros, listed among the descendants of Mizraim.
draft.evidence: Genesis 10:13–14 and 1 Chronicles 1:11–12 name the Pathrusim in the same sequence of peoples. Jeremiah 44:1 places the land of Pathros in Egypt.

analysis.evidence: וְאֶת פַּתְרֻסִים continues the list governed by וּמִצְרַיִם יָלַד, “and Mizraim fathered,” in Genesis 10:13. The same genealogy names the Pathrusim immediately before the Casluhim in 1 Chronicles 1:12. The gentilic corresponds to פַּתְרוֹס, Pathros, a region of Egypt named in Jeremiah 44:1.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew gentilic noun, masculine plural absolute. The plural ending ־ִים is part of the noun. The preceding וְאֶת is a separate word.
analysis.sense: The people of Pathros, counted among the descendants of Mizraim.

draft.change: Add a noun article for the gentilic כַּסְלֻחִים. Its consonantal stem is כסלח. A derivation from כסל is unestablished.
draft.definition: The Casluhim, a people descended from Mizraim.
draft.evidence: Genesis 10:13–14 and 1 Chronicles 1:11–12 both place the Casluhim after the Pathrusim in the genealogy of Mizraim.

analysis.evidence: The list governed by וּמִצְרַיִם יָלַד in Genesis 10:13 continues in verse 14. The repeated וְאֶת introduces כַּסְלֻחִים as the next people after the Pathrusim. The following clause says that the Philistines came from there.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew gentilic noun, masculine plural absolute. The ending ־ִים marks the plural. The preceding וְאֶת is a separate word.
analysis.sense: A people counted among the descendants of Mizraim.

analysis.morphology: Indeclinable relative particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In יָצְאוּ מִשָּׁם פְּלִשְׁתִּים, the Philistines are the ones who came forth. מִשָּׁם means “from there” and points back to the Casluhim. In this genealogy, the clause traces the Philistines’ origin.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person common plural, agreeing with the following subject פְּלִשְׁתִּים.
analysis.sense: come forth from an ancestral people

analysis.evidence: In אֲשֶׁר יָצְאוּ מִשָּׁם פְּלִשְׁתִּים, “from there the Philistines came,” פְּלִשְׁתִּים names the people who came from there and serves as the subject of the plural verb יָצְאוּ.
analysis.morphology: Gentilic adjective used as a noun, masculine plural absolute, with no prefix or pronominal suffix.
